title: 10.1–10.3 Catch-Up
contentObjective: I can show I am caught up on Lessons 10.1–10.3 by using each lesson's big idea in mixed practice.
languageObjective: I can explain which lesson's big idea I used and how, using key vocabulary from Lessons 10.1–10.3.

vocabulary.definition: A job someone is trained to do, like chef, nurse, or carpenter.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un trabajo para el que alguien se ha preparado, como chef, enfermero o carpintero.
vocabulary.example: Chefs are found in restaurant kitchens overseeing food preparation.
vocabulary.visual: A chef prices a menu; a nurse measures a dose; a carpenter cuts to length.
vocabulary.cloze: A job someone is trained to do, like chef or nurse, is a ___.

examples.text: A chef planning portions for 120 guests
examples.why: It is trained work, and it uses math.

examples.text: A hobby you do on weekends
examples.why: A hobby is not the job someone trained for.

vocabulary.definition: The supply of items a business keeps on hand, tracked by counting.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Las existencias que un negocio tiene disponibles, controladas contándolas.
vocabulary.example: A chef manages inventory so the kitchen never runs out of ingredients.
vocabulary.visual: The kitchen counts 40 lb of flour and 12 dozen eggs on hand.
vocabulary.cloze: The supply a business keeps on hand, tracked by counting, is its ___.

examples.text: A list of what is in stock this morning
examples.why: It counts what the business actually has.
Prices are what things cost, not what is in stock.

vocabulary.definition: The measured amount of food served to one person.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La cantidad medida de comida que se sirve a una persona.
vocabulary.example: Chefs decide on the portion size of each item on the menu.
vocabulary.visual: Each bowl of soup uses 2 cups of broth — one person's serving.
vocabulary.cloze: The measured amount of food served to one person is a ___.

examples.why: It is the amount one person receives.
That is a count of people, not an amount of food.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of flat space a surface covers, measured in square units.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La cantidad de espacio plano que cubre una superficie, medida en unidades cuadradas.
vocabulary.example: Gardeners calculate the area of the planter to decide how many plants fit.
vocabulary.visual: A 4 ft by 2 ft planter covers 8 square feet of ground.
vocabulary.cloze: The flat space a surface covers, in square units, is its ___.

examples.text: The square feet of floor in a store space
examples.why: It measures flat space, in square units.

examples.text: The soil that fills the planter
examples.why: Filling a space is volume, in cubic units.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of space something fills, measured in cubic units.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La cantidad de espacio que algo ocupa, medida en unidades cúbicas.
vocabulary.example: Gardeners calculate the volume of the planter to know how much soil to buy.
vocabulary.visual: 4 ft × 2 ft × 1 ft of soil = 8 cubic feet.
vocabulary.cloze: The space something fills, in cubic units, is its ___.

examples.text: The soil needed to fill a planter
examples.why: It fills a space, so it is measured in cubic units.

examples.text: The paper needed to wrap the planter
examples.why: Covering the outside is surface area.

vocabulary.definition: Having two halves that match — one side is a mirror image of the other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Que tiene dos mitades que coinciden: un lado es la imagen reflejada del otro.
vocabulary.example: The two sides of the butterfly look like mirror images. The butterfly is symmetric.
vocabulary.visual: A butterfly: the left wing is the mirror of the right.
vocabulary.cloze: Having two halves that match as mirror images is being ___.

examples.why: One side reflects the other exactly.

examples.text: A brightly coloured but lopsided leaf
examples.why: Colour is not the test — matching halves are.

vocabulary.definition: A copy of a figure flipped across a line, so the two halves face each other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una copia de una figura volteada al otro lado de una línea, de modo que las dos mitades se miran entre sí.
vocabulary.example: The left wing of a butterfly is a mirror image of the right wing.
vocabulary.visual: Fold the layer down the middle: each leaf lands on its partner.
vocabulary.cloze: A copy of a figure flipped across a line is its ___ ___.

examples.text: The right half of a butterfly compared to the left
examples.why: Flipping one across the line gives the other.

examples.text: The same shape slid to the side
examples.why: Sliding is not flipping — nothing is reversed.

vocabulary.definition: Reflective symmetry in plants and animals — the two sides of the body mirror each other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La simetría reflectiva en plantas y animales: los dos lados del cuerpo se reflejan entre sí.
vocabulary.example: All butterflies have reflective symmetry; in plants and animals this is called bilateral symmetry.
vocabulary.visual: All 17,000+ butterfly species have it — two sides, one mirror line.
vocabulary.cloze: Reflective symmetry in plants and animals is called ___ ___.

examples.text: A flower whose two halves mirror across a slanted line
examples.why: The direction of the line does not matter.

examples.text: A leaf with more veins on one side
examples.why: The halves do not match, so nothing mirrors.

vocabulary.definition: A problem designed to be played with — it has rules, a goal, and room to imagine solutions.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un problema diseñado para jugarse: tiene reglas, una meta y espacio para imaginar soluciones.
vocabulary.example: The Tower of Hanoi is a puzzle that was invented in 1883.
vocabulary.visual: Tower of Hanoi: three rods, a stack of discs, and two rules.
vocabulary.cloze: A problem designed to be played with — rules, a goal, room to imagine — is a ___.

examples.text: Moving a tower of discs without stacking big on small
examples.why: It has rules, a goal, and many ways in.

examples.text: A page of the same computation twenty times
examples.why: There is nothing to figure out, only to repeat.

launch.narrative: Missed a lesson — or just want a refresher? This catch-up station reviews Lessons 10.1–10.3: 10.1 Math is Everywhere, 10.2 Math is Beauty, 10.3 Math is Playful. Read the Big Ideas, warm up with the review problem, then prove you're caught up in the mixed practice.

conceptIntro.heading: The Big Ideas — Lessons 10.1–10.3
conceptIntro.intro: Here is the one thing to remember from each lesson, plus a quick guided example. If one of these feels shaky, that lesson is right above this one in the menu — you can open it any time.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 10.1: People use math every day in their professions and their hobbies — and it is a good tool for solving problems around your house, too. • 10.2: Bilateral symmetry — two sides that are mirror images — appears throughout nature, and it shapes human creations from art to music to architecture. • 10.3: We play with math by using our imagination and by looking for patterns or relationships that help us think logically — a pattern can tell us the answer to a puzzle we have not even played yet.

iDo.title: The Big Ideas (one per lesson)
lines: Lesson 10.1 — Math is Everywhere: People use math every day in their professions and their hobbies — and it is a good tool for solving problems around your house, too.
Lesson 10.2 — Math is Beauty: Bilateral symmetry — two sides that are mirror images — appears throughout nature, and it shapes human creations from art to music to architecture.

Lesson 10.3 — Math is Playful: We play with math by using our imagination and by looking for patterns or relationships that help us think logically — a pattern can tell us the answer to a puzzle we have not even played yet.
linesEs: Lección 10.1 — Las matemáticas están en todas partes: La gente usa las matemáticas todos los días en sus profesiones y en sus pasatiempos — y también son una buena herramienta para resolver problemas en tu casa.

Lección 10.2 — Las matemáticas son belleza: La simetría bilateral — dos lados que son imágenes en espejo — aparece por toda la naturaleza, y le da forma a las creaciones humanas, del arte a la música y la arquitectura.

Lección 10.3 — Las matemáticas son juego: Jugamos con las matemáticas usando la imaginación y buscando patrones o relaciones que nos ayuden a pensar con lógica — un patrón nos puede decir la respuesta de un rompecabezas que ni siquiera hemos jugado.

weDo.title: Quick guided checks — one from each lesson
lines: From 10.1: A planter that is 4 feet long and 2 feet wide has an area of 4 × 2 = 8 square feet — that tells us how many plants fit.
From 10.2: This plant grows in layers, and each layer is made up of two leaves — so 3 layers hold 3 × 2 = 6 leaves.
From 10.3: Discs: 1, 2, 3 — Steps: 1, 3, 7. What is happening from each row to the next?
linesEs: De 10.1: Una jardinera de 4 pies de largo y 2 pies de ancho tiene un área de 4 × 2 = 8 pies cuadrados — eso nos dice cuántas plantas caben.
De 10.2: Esta planta crece por capas, y cada capa está formada por dos hojas — así que 3 capas tienen 3 × 2 = 6 hojas.
De 10.3: Discos: 1, 2, 3 — Pasos: 1, 3, 7. ¿Qué pasa de una fila a la siguiente?

explore.label: Legal move or against the rules? Sort each Tower of Hanoi move.

cards.text: Move the top disc of a stack to an empty rod
Place a small disc on top of a larger disc
Move one disc at a time
Move the smallest disc back to the rod it came from earlier
Place a larger disc on top of a smaller disc
Move two discs together in one move
Pull out a disc from the middle of a stack
Add a fourth rod to make the puzzle easier

explore.instructions: The rules are the whole game: one disc at a time, only the top disc of a stack, and a larger disc can never sit on a smaller disc. After sorting, tell a partner which rule is hardest to obey when you actually play.

connect.scenario: You solved the small towers by hand: 1 disc takes 1 step, 2 discs take 3 steps, 3 discs take 7 steps. Now someone hands you a five-disc tower and asks for the fewest steps — but you do not have time to play it out.
connect.promptQuestion: How can a pattern help you imagine the solution?
connect.prompt: The pattern rule for the Tower of Hanoi is to ___ the number of steps for the smaller tower and ___ for each new disc. Applying this rule twice starting from 7 steps for a three-disc tower gives a five-disc tower a minimum of ___ steps.

check.stem: The table shows: 1 disc = 1 step, 2 discs = 3 steps, 3 discs = 7 steps. What is the pattern rule from one row to the next?
choices: Add 2 to the previous number of steps
Double the previous number of steps and add 1
Multiply the previous number of steps by 3
Add the disc number to the previous steps
check.explanation: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3 and 3 × 2 + 1 = 7, so the rule is double and add 1. Adding 2 matches 1→3 but fails on 3→5≠7, multiplying by 3 matches 1→3 but fails on 3→9≠7, and adding the disc number matches 1+2=3 but fails on 3+3=6≠7.

check.stem: Using the rule "double the steps and add 1," how many steps does a 4-disc tower take, starting from the 3-disc value of 7 steps?
check.explanation: 7 × 2 + 1 = 15. 8 comes from only adding 1 without doubling, 14 comes from only doubling without adding 1, and 21 comes from tripling instead of doubling.

check.stem: Continuing the pattern from 15 steps for a 4-disc tower, how many steps does a 5-disc tower take?
check.explanation: 15 × 2 + 1 = 31. 16 comes from only adding 1, 30 comes from only doubling, and 45 comes from tripling 15 instead of doubling and adding 1.

connect.modelAnswer: I would organize what I know in a table: 1 disc takes 1 step, 2 discs take 3, 3 discs take 7. The pattern rule is to double the number of steps and add 1 for each new disc. So 4 discs take 7 × 2 + 1 = 15 steps, and 5 discs take 15 × 2 + 1 = 31 steps. The pattern let me imagine the solution — a minimum of 31 steps — without ever touching the discs.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 10.1) A planter is 4 feet long and 2 feet wide. What is its area?
approaching.explanation: Area of a rectangle is length × width: 4 × 2 = 8 square feet.
choiceFeedback: 6 comes from adding 4 + 2 instead of multiplying.
12 comes from adding all four sides (4 + 2 + 4 + 2) — that is the perimeter, not the area.
2 comes from dividing 4 by 2 instead of multiplying.
hints: Area tells how much flat space the planter covers.
For a rectangle, multiply length by width.
Multiply 4 × 2.
approaching.stemEs: Una jardinera mide 4 pies de largo y 2 pies de ancho. ¿Cuál es su área?
approaching.explanationEs: El área de un rectángulo es largo × ancho: 4 × 2 = 8 pies cuadrados.
hintsEs: El área dice cuánto espacio plano cubre la jardinera.
Para un rectángulo, multiplica largo por ancho.
Multiplica 4 × 2.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 10.1) That same planter is 4 feet long, 2 feet wide, and needs soil 1 foot deep. How much soil does the gardener need?
approaching.explanation: Volume is length × width × depth: 4 × 2 × 1 = 8 cubic feet of soil.
choiceFeedback: 7 comes from adding 4 + 2 + 1 instead of multiplying.
The number is right but soil fills space, so volume needs cubic units, not square units.
4 forgets to multiply by the width of 2.
hints: Soil fills space, so you need volume.
Volume of a box is length × width × depth.
Multiply 4 × 2 × 1.
approaching.stemEs: Esa misma jardinera mide 4 pies de largo, 2 pies de ancho y necesita tierra de 1 pie de profundidad. ¿Cuánta tierra necesita el jardinero?
approaching.explanationEs: El volumen es largo × ancho × profundidad: 4 × 2 × 1 = 8 pies cúbicos de tierra.
hintsEs: La tierra llena espacio, así que necesitas el volumen.
El volumen de una caja es largo × ancho × profundidad.
Multiplica 4 × 2 × 1.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 10.2) What does it mean that a butterfly is symmetric?
choices: The two sides of the butterfly look like mirror images
The butterfly has exactly two wings
The butterfly's wings are very colorful
The butterfly is larger than most insects
approaching.explanation: Symmetric means one side is a mirror image of the other — that is exactly what we see across the butterfly's body.
choiceFeedback: Having two wings is not enough — the two sides must MIRROR each other to be symmetric.
Color makes a butterfly pretty, but symmetry is about the two sides matching, not about color.
Size has nothing to do with symmetry — a tiny butterfly is just as symmetric as a big one.
hints: Think about what you see on the left wing versus the right wing.
Imagine a mirror standing along the butterfly's body.
What word describes two sides that reflect each other?
approaching.stemEs: ¿Qué significa que una mariposa sea simétrica?
approaching.explanationEs: Simétrico significa que un lado es imagen reflejada del otro — eso es exactamente lo que vemos a ambos lados del cuerpo de la mariposa.
hintsEs: Piensa en lo que ves en el ala izquierda comparado con el ala derecha.
Imagina un espejo colocado a lo largo del cuerpo de la mariposa.
¿Qué palabra describe dos lados que se reflejan entre sí?
choicesEs: Los dos lados de la mariposa se ven como imágenes reflejadas
La mariposa tiene exactamente dos alas
Las alas de la mariposa son muy coloridas
La mariposa es más grande que la mayoría de los insectos

approaching.stem: (Lesson 10.2) In plants and animals, reflective symmetry is called:
approaching.explanation: The lesson says it directly: all butterflies have reflective symmetry, and in plants and animals this is called bilateral symmetry.
choiceFeedback: Rotational symmetry is about turning a shape, not reflecting it across a line.
A mirror image is what each SIDE is — the name for the whole property in living things is different.
Balance is why our brains find symmetry pleasing, not the name of the symmetry itself.
hints: The word starts with 'bi-', meaning two.
It describes the two sides of a body.
Bi-lateral means two-sided.
approaching.stemEs: En plantas y animales, la simetría de reflexión se llama:
approaching.explanationEs: La lección lo dice directamente: todas las mariposas tienen simetría de reflexión, y en plantas y animales esto se llama simetría bilateral.
hintsEs: La palabra empieza con 'bi-', que significa dos.
Describe los dos lados de un cuerpo.
Bi-lateral significa de dos lados.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 10.3) What is the fewest number of moves needed to solve a three-disc Tower of Hanoi puzzle?
approaching.explanation: It takes at least 7 moves to solve a three-disc Tower of Hanoi puzzle.
choiceFeedback: 3 is the number of DISCS — moving each disc only once is impossible because of the size rule.
6 doubles the 3 discs but forgets the extra move — the pattern is double and add 1, so 3 discs need 7.
9 is 3 × 3, but the fewest-moves count follows the doubling pattern, not disc × disc.
hints: It is more than one move per disc.
A two-disc tower already takes 3 moves.
Double 3 and add 1.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál es el menor número de movimientos necesarios para resolver la Torre de Hanói de tres discos?
approaching.explanationEs: Se necesitan al menos 7 movimientos para resolver la Torre de Hanói de tres discos.
hintsEs: Es más de un movimiento por disco.
Una torre de dos discos ya toma 3 movimientos.
Duplica 3 y suma 1.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 10.3) Which move is against the rules of the Tower of Hanoi?
choices: Placing a larger disc on top of a smaller disc
Moving one disc at a time
Moving the top disc from a stack
Placing a smaller disc on top of a larger disc
approaching.explanation: A larger disc can never be on top of a smaller disc — that is the rule that makes the puzzle a puzzle.
choiceFeedback: One disc at a time is exactly what the rules require, not what they forbid.
You may only move the TOP disc of a stack — that move follows the rules.
Smaller on top of larger is the legal direction; it is the reverse that is banned.
hints: Two of these are the rules themselves.
Think about disc SIZES.
Which stacking order would crush a smaller disc?
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál movimiento va contra las reglas de la Torre de Hanói?
approaching.explanationEs: Un disco más grande nunca puede estar sobre uno más pequeño — esa es la regla que hace que el rompecabezas sea un rompecabezas.
hintsEs: Dos de estas son las reglas mismas.
Piensa en los TAMAÑOS de los discos.
¿Cuál orden de apilado aplastaría un disco más pequeño?
choicesEs: Poner un disco más grande sobre uno más pequeño
Mover un disco a la vez
Mover el disco de arriba de una pila
Poner un disco más pequeño sobre uno más grande

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 10.1) One person saves 8 gallons of water a day by turning the water on only to rinse. How much water does that person save in a year (365 days)?
onLevel.explanation: 8 gallons a day × 365 days = 2,920 gallons in a year.
choiceFeedback: 373 comes from adding 8 + 365 instead of multiplying.
1,460 multiplies 365 by 4 — the savings from one brushing — instead of the full 8 gallons a day.
365 is just the number of days; it forgets to multiply by the gallons saved each day.
hints: You know the savings per day.
How many days are in a year?
Multiply 8 × 365.
onLevel.stemEs: Una persona ahorra 8 galones de agua al día al abrir la llave solo para enjuagar. ¿Cuánta agua ahorra esa persona en un año (365 días)?
onLevel.explanationEs: 8 galones al día × 365 días = 2,920 galones en un año.
hintsEs: Conoces el ahorro por día.
¿Cuántos días tiene un año?
Multiplica 8 × 365.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 10.1) If each person in a house saves 2,920 gallons a year, how much does a household of 3 people save in a year?
onLevel.explanation: 2,920 gallons per person × 3 people = 8,760 gallons a year.
choiceFeedback: 2,923 comes from adding 2,920 + 3 instead of multiplying.
973 (about 2,920 ÷ 3) divides instead of multiplying — more people save MORE water, not less.
5,840 multiplies by 2 people instead of 3.
hints: Each person saves the same amount.
3 people, each saving 2,920 gallons.
Multiply 2,920 × 3.
onLevel.stemEs: Si cada persona de una casa ahorra 2,920 galones al año, ¿cuánto ahorra en un año un hogar de 3 personas?
onLevel.explanationEs: 2,920 galones por persona × 3 personas = 8,760 galones al año.
hintsEs: Cada persona ahorra la misma cantidad.
3 personas, cada una ahorrando 2,920 galones.
Multiplica 2,920 × 3.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 10.2) Why do people find symmetry pleasing?
choices: Our brains are wired to favor balance, and bilateral symmetry provides balance
Symmetric things are always brightly colored
Symmetry only appears in rare and expensive objects
Symmetric shapes are always larger than non-symmetric ones
onLevel.explanation: The lesson says it directly: our brains are wired to favor balance, and bilateral symmetry provides balance.
choiceFeedback: Color is separate from symmetry — a plain gray moth can be perfectly symmetric.
Symmetry is everywhere in nature, from leaves to ladybugs — it is common, not rare.
Size has nothing to do with it — a tiny symmetric leaf is as balanced as a huge one.
hints: The answer is about how our brains respond.
What does bilateral symmetry provide that brains favor?
Think of an even, steady arrangement.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Por qué a las personas les agrada la simetría?
onLevel.explanationEs: La lección lo dice directamente: nuestro cerebro está hecho para preferir el equilibrio, y la simetría bilateral da equilibrio.
hintsEs: La respuesta tiene que ver con cómo responde nuestro cerebro.
¿Qué proporciona la simetría bilateral que el cerebro prefiere?
Piensa en un arreglo parejo y constante.
choicesEs: Nuestro cerebro está hecho para preferir el equilibrio, y la simetría bilateral da equilibrio
Las cosas simétricas siempre tienen colores brillantes
La simetría solo aparece en objetos raros y caros
Las figuras simétricas siempre son más grandes que las no simétricas

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 10.2) There are over 17,000 species of butterflies, and ALL butterflies have reflective symmetry. About how many of those species have reflective symmetry?
choices: None — symmetry is only in plants
onLevel.explanation: 'All butterflies have reflective symmetry' means every one of the 17,000+ species — no exceptions.
choiceFeedback: 'All' means every single species, not half of them.
Symmetry is about the two sides matching, not about how colorful the wings are.
The butterfly itself was our first example — animals show bilateral symmetry too.
hints: Read the statement carefully: ALL butterflies.
Does 'all' leave any out?
Every species means every species.
onLevel.stemEs: Hay más de 17,000 especies de mariposas, y TODAS las mariposas tienen simetría de reflexión. ¿Aproximadamente cuántas de esas especies tienen simetría de reflexión?
onLevel.explanationEs: 'Todas las mariposas tienen simetría de reflexión' significa cada una de las más de 17,000 especies — sin excepciones.
hintsEs: Lee el enunciado con cuidado: TODAS las mariposas.
¿'Todas' deja alguna fuera?
Cada especie significa cada especie.
choicesEs: Ninguna — la simetría solo está en las plantas

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 10.3) The table shows 1 disc → 1 step, 2 discs → 3 steps, 3 discs → 7 steps. What is the pattern rule for the number of steps when you add one more disc?
choices: Double the number of steps and add 1
Add 2 to the number of steps
Add the number of discs to the steps
Multiply the number of steps by 3
onLevel.explanation: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3 and 3 × 2 + 1 = 7, so each new disc doubles the steps and adds 1.
choiceFeedback: Adding 2 fits 1 → 3 but fails the next row: 3 + 2 = 5, and the table says 7.
Adding the discs fits 1 → 3 (1 + 2) but fails the next row: 3 + 3 = 6, and the table says 7.
Multiplying by 3 fits 1 → 3 but fails the next row: 3 × 3 = 9, and the table says 7.
hints: Test each rule on BOTH jumps: 1 → 3 and 3 → 7.
Several rules pass the first jump; only one passes both.
What do you do to 3 to land exactly on 7?
onLevel.stemEs: La tabla muestra 1 disco → 1 paso, 2 discos → 3 pasos, 3 discos → 7 pasos. ¿Cuál es la regla del patrón para el número de pasos cuando agregas un disco más?
onLevel.explanationEs: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3 y 3 × 2 + 1 = 7, así que cada disco nuevo duplica los pasos y suma 1.
hintsEs: Prueba cada regla en LOS DOS saltos: 1 → 3 y 3 → 7.
Varias reglas pasan el primer salto; solo una pasa los dos.
¿Qué le haces al 3 para caer exactamente en 7?
choicesEs: Duplicar el número de pasos y sumar 1
Suma el número de discos a los pasos
Multiplicar el número de pasos por 3

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 10.3) Use the pattern rule to complete the table: how many steps for a four-disc tower?
onLevel.explanation: A three-disc tower takes 7 steps, so a four-disc tower takes 7 × 2 + 1 = 15 steps.
choiceFeedback: 14 doubles the 7 steps but forgets to add 1.
9 adds 2 to 7 instead of doubling and adding 1.
28 multiplies 7 by 4 (the number of discs) instead of doubling once and adding 1.
hints: Start from the three-disc answer: 7 steps.
Apply the rule: double, then add 1.
onLevel.stemEs: Usa la regla del patrón para completar la tabla: ¿cuántos pasos para una torre de cuatro discos?
onLevel.explanationEs: Una torre de tres discos toma 7 pasos, así que una torre de cuatro discos toma 7 × 2 + 1 = 15 pasos.
hintsEs: Empieza con la respuesta de tres discos: 7 pasos.
Aplica la regla: duplica y luego suma 1.

onLevel.title: Fix our table's thinking

workedExample.label: The problem
workedExample.work: (Lesson 10.3) What is the fewest number of moves needed to solve a three-disc Tower of Hanoi puzzle?
workedExample.workEs: ¿Cuál es el menor número de movimientos necesarios para resolver la Torre de Hanói de tres discos?

workedExample.label: A classmate at our table answered
workedExample.labelEs: Un compañero de nuestra mesa respondió

onLevel.correctWork: The correct answer is 7 moves. It takes at least 7 moves to solve a three-disc Tower of Hanoi puzzle.
onLevel.correctWorkEs: La respuesta correcta es 7 movimientos. Se necesitan al menos 7 movimientos para resolver la Torre de Hanói de tres discos.
hints: It is more than one move per disc.
hintsEs: Es más de un movimiento por disco.

extending.stem: (Lesson 10.1) Each person saves 2,920 gallons a year. Which correctly compares households of 3, 4, 5, and 8 people?
extending.explanation: Multiply 2,920 by each household size. For 3 people: 3 × 2,920 = 8,760. For 4 and 5 people: 11,680 and 14,600. For 8 people: 8 × 2,920 = 23,360.
choiceFeedback: 20,440 is 7 × 2,920 — the last household has 8 people, not 7.
Those add the household size to 2,920 instead of multiplying by it.
46,720 is 16 × 2,920 — that doubles the 8-person household instead of computing it.
hints: Each household total is people × 2,920.
Check the last value most carefully.
extending.stemEs: Cada persona ahorra 2,920 galones al año. ¿Cuál compara correctamente hogares de 3, 4, 5 y 8 personas?
extending.explanationEs: Multiplica 2,920 por cada tamaño de hogar. Para 3 personas: 3 × 2,920 = 8,760. Para 4 y 5 personas: 11,680 y 14,600. Para 8 personas: 8 × 2,920 = 23,360.
hintsEs: El total de cada hogar es personas × 2,920.
Revisa el último valor con más cuidado.

extending.stem: (Lesson 10.2) Your friend insists that only ONE of two flowers has bilateral symmetry, but both pass the mirror-image test — just across lines pointing in different directions. What is the best response?
choices: Both flowers have bilateral symmetry — a line of symmetry does not have to point the same direction in every figure
Your friend is right, because a real line of symmetry must always be vertical
Neither flower has bilateral symmetry, because flowers are not animals
Agree with your friend, because two people should not disagree about math
extending.explanation: The test for bilateral symmetry is whether SOME line makes the two sides mirror images — the direction of that line does not matter.
choiceFeedback: Nothing in the definition requires vertical — a mirror line can run in any direction.
Plants have bilateral symmetry too; the leaf layers in this very lesson were the example.
Math disagreements are settled with evidence and a test, not with politeness.
hints: Apply the same test to both flowers.
Does the definition say which direction the line must point?
If a mirror line exists, the symmetry exists.
extending.stemEs: Tu amigo insiste en que solo UNA de dos flores tiene simetría bilateral, pero ambas pasan la prueba de la imagen reflejada — solo que con líneas que apuntan en direcciones distintas. ¿Cuál es la mejor respuesta?
extending.explanationEs: La prueba de la simetría bilateral es si ALGUNA línea hace que los dos lados sean imágenes reflejadas — la dirección de esa línea no importa.
hintsEs: Aplica la misma prueba a las dos flores.
¿La definición dice en qué dirección debe apuntar la línea?
Si existe un eje de reflexión, existe la simetría.
choicesEs: Ambas flores tienen simetría bilateral — un eje de simetría no tiene que apuntar en la misma dirección en cada figura
Tu amigo tiene razón, porque un eje de simetría verdadero siempre debe ser vertical
Ninguna flor tiene simetría bilateral, porque las flores no son animales
Estar de acuerdo con tu amigo, porque dos personas no deberían estar en desacuerdo sobre matemáticas

extending.stem: (Lesson 10.3) A five-disc tower takes 31 steps. Using the pattern rule, how many steps would a SIX-disc tower take?
extending.explanation: Apply the rule to 31: double it and add 1, so 31 × 2 + 1 = 63 steps.
choiceFeedback: 62 doubles the 31 steps but forgets to add 1.
36 adds 5 to 31 — the rule doubles the steps rather than adding the disc count.
32 adds 1 to 31 but forgets to double first.
hints: The rule works from any row of the table.
Double, then add 1.
extending.stemEs: Una torre de cinco discos toma 31 pasos. Usando la regla del patrón, ¿cuántos pasos tomaría una torre de SEIS discos?
extending.explanationEs: Aplica la regla a 31: duplícalo y suma 1, así que 31 × 2 + 1 = 63 pasos.
hintsEs: La regla funciona desde cualquier fila de la tabla.
Duplica y luego suma 1.

optional.instructions: (Lesson 10.1) The gardener plans a 4 ft by 2 ft planter that is 1 ft deep. Sort each question: area or volume?
optional.instructionsEs: El jardinero planea un cantero de 4 pies por 2 pies con 1 pie de profundidad. Clasifica cada pregunta: ¿área o volumen?
optional.label: Sort each gardening question: does it need area or volume?
optional.labelEs: Clasifica cada pregunta de jardinería: ¿necesita área o volumen?

categories.label: Area (square feet)
items: How much ground does the planter cover?
How much mesh covers the top against birds?
How much of the yard is left uncovered?
itemsEs: ¿Cuánta malla cubre la parte de arriba contra los pájaros?

categories.label: Volume (cubic feet)
items: How much soil fills the planter?
How much compost fills a second, deeper planter?
How much water does the full rain barrel hold?
itemsEs: ¿Cuánta composta llena un segundo cantero más profundo?
¿Cuánta agua cabe en el barril de lluvia lleno?

hints: Covering flat ground is area; filling a container is volume.
The planter's 4 × 2 base covers 8 square feet; add the 1-foot depth and the soil is 8 cubic feet.
hintsEs: Cubrir terreno plano es área; llenar un recipiente es volumen.
La base de 4 × 2 del cantero son 8 pies cuadrados; con 1 pie de profundidad, la tierra son 8 pies cúbicos.
optional.explanation: The gardener needs both measures for one planter: covering questions (ground, mesh, yard) are flat and use square feet, while filling questions (soil, compost, water) use all three dimensions and cubic feet. Choosing the right measure before computing is the real-world modeling step.
optional.explanationEs: El jardinero necesita ambas medidas para un solo cantero: las preguntas de cubrir (terreno, malla, patio) son planas y usan pies cuadrados, mientras que las de llenar (tierra, composta, agua) usan las tres dimensiones y pies cúbicos. Elegir la medida correcta antes de calcular es el paso de modelado del mundo real.

practice.commonMistake: Doubling the previous number of steps but forgetting to add 1 — answering 14 instead of 15 for four discs, or 30 instead of 31 for five.

diagram.title: Fewest Moves in Tower of Hanoi
diagram.caption: Each bar doubles the one before it and adds 1: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31. One more disc nearly doubles the work, so the bars grow far faster than the disc count.

optionalActivity.name: Catch-Up Challenge
optionalActivity.intro: Mix it up: pick the right lesson's big idea for each problem — that's the real catch-up skill.

exitTicket.stem: (Catch-up check, from Lesson 10.2) Which statement best shows what this lesson means by 'math is beauty'?
choices: Math creates beautiful designs like bilateral symmetry, found in nature and used in human art, music, and architecture
Only things made by mathematicians can be beautiful
Butterflies are the only living things with symmetry
Beauty and math are opposites — one is feeling and one is numbers
exitTicket.explanation: The summary makes the claim in two parts. Bilateral symmetry appears naturally in many plants and animals. It also influences human creations. You can see it in art, in music, and in architecture.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It mentions nature AND human creations.
Which option includes both?

questions.stem: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
questions.explanation: A square folds onto itself along both diagonals and both midlines — 4 lines in all.
questions.stemEs: ¿Cuántos ejes de simetría tiene un cuadrado?
questions.explanationEs: Un cuadrado se dobla sobre sí mismo por las dos diagonales y las dos líneas medias — 4 ejes en total.

questions.stem: A shape has bilateral symmetry. This means…
choices: one line splits it into two mirror halves
it can be turned in a circle
questions.explanation: Bilateral symmetry means a single line divides the shape into halves that mirror each other.
questions.stemEs: Una figura tiene simetría bilateral. Eso significa que…
choicesEs: un eje la divide en dos mitades que son imágenes en espejo
questions.explanationEs: La simetría bilateral significa que un solo eje divide la figura en mitades que se reflejan entre sí.

questions.stem: Which capital letter has a vertical line of symmetry?
questions.explanation: A folds onto itself along a vertical line down its middle. R, P and F do not.
questions.stemEs: ¿Qué letra mayúscula tiene un eje de simetría vertical?
questions.explanationEs: La A se dobla sobre sí misma por un eje vertical que pasa por su centro. La R, la P y la F no.

questions.stem: How many lines of symmetry does a regular hexagon have?
questions.explanation: A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry — one through each pair of opposite vertices and each pair of opposite sides.
questions.stemEs: ¿Cuántos ejes de simetría tiene un hexágono regular?
questions.explanationEs: Un hexágono regular tiene 6 ejes de simetría — uno por cada par de vértices opuestos y cada par de lados opuestos.
